text:
**The Unraveling Mystery**
Have you ever pulled a single loose thread from your favorite shirt, only to watch the whole garment slowly start to unravel? Why does pulling one tiny thread cause the entire piece of clothing to fall apart? What exactly is holding it all together?

**A Socratic Puzzle**
If a shirt is just a collection of intersecting threads, what are those individual threads made of? Can you imagine breaking a single, tiny thread down even further into something smaller?

content.title: Untwisting the Rope
content.description: Imagine a thick rope used for tug-of-war. If you untwist it, you see smaller cords. Untwist those, and you get tiny, hair-like strands. A piece of cloth works in the exact same way!

text:
**The Reveal: Fibre, Yarn, Fabric**
The beautiful clothes we wear are made of **Fabrics**. If you look closely, fabrics are made of intersecting threads called **Yarns**. If you untwist a yarn, you will find it is made of even thinner, hair-like strands called **Fibres**. Therefore, the sequence is: Fibres are spun into Yarns, and Yarns are woven into Fabric.

content.preview: The thinnest, hair-like strands that are spun together to make yarn.
A continuous spun thread made from fibres, used for weaving or knitting fabrics.

content.question: What is the correct sequence of making cloth?

content.text: Remember the order using alphabetical logic: **F**ibre (starts with F, smallest), then **Y**arn (Y is near the end), but wait, that doesn't work! Better yet, think of building a house: Fibres are the bricks, Yarns are the walls, and Fabric is the complete house.
Students often confuse 'Fibre' and 'Fabric'. Remember, **Fabric** is the final cloth you wear, while **Fibre** is the tiny raw material it starts from.

text:
**Reflection**
Look closely at the shirt or dress you are wearing right now. Can you spot the tiny yarns woven together in a crisscross pattern? Imagine how many millions of fibres it took to make your single outfit!

**Connection to the Knowledge Graph**
This concept of smaller units building larger structures is everywhere! In biology, tiny *Cells* build *Tissues*, which build *Organs*. In chemistry, *Atoms* build *Molecules*. Here, *Fibres* build *Yarns*, which build *Fabrics*.

content.title: Mastery Challenge: The Yarn Extractor
content.instructions: Take a small, unwanted scrap of cotton cloth. Use a pin to gently pull out a single yarn from the edge. Then, try to untwist that single yarn with your fingers. You will see the incredibly thin, fuzzy cotton fibres! You have successfully reverse-engineered fabric.

text:
**The Mystery of the Ancients**
In ancient India, thousands of years before modern factories and synthetic chemicals were invented, people wore beautifully woven garments. Where did they find the materials to make these clothes?

**Socratic Question: Nature's Gifts**
If you were stranded in a dense forest and needed to make clothes, where would you look? Would you look at the plants around you, or perhaps the animals?

content.title: Nature vs Lab
content.description: Visualizing the origin of fibres: A cotton plant blooming vs a chemical factory producing nylon.

text:
**The Reveal: Natural vs Synthetic Fibres**
Fibres are classified based on where they come from. Fibres obtained from nature (plants and animals) are called **Natural Fibres** (e.g., Cotton and Jute from plants; Wool and Silk from animals). Fibres made by humans using chemicals in factories are called **Synthetic Fibres** (e.g., Nylon, Polyester, Acrylic).

content.preview: Fibres that are obtained directly from plants or animals.
Artificial fibres manufactured in factories using chemical processes.

text:
**Reflection**
Why do we prefer wearing cotton clothes during the hot Indian summer, but switch to woolen sweaters in the freezing winter? How do the properties of these natural fibres help our bodies?

**Connection to History**
Ancient Indian texts like the *Rigveda* mention weaving and the use of cotton. India was the birthplace of cotton cultivation, and our ancient ancestors mastered the art of spinning natural plant fibres into exquisite fabrics long before the rest of the world!

content.title: Mastery Challenge: The Wardrobe Detective
content.instructions: Open your wardrobe and look at the tiny white tags on the inside of 3 different shirts or pants. Read the material composition (e.g., '100% Cotton' or '60% Polyester, 40% Cotton'). Classify each garment as Natural, Synthetic, or a Blend!
